title: WHO / IDF Clinical Reference Thresholds for Diabetes Screening
scope_note: Cut-off values used to interpret the 8 clinical parameters accepted by this application. These are screening-interpretation aids, not diagnostic criteria. A clinical diagnosis of diabetes requires laboratory confirmation by a licensed practitioner.

risk_bands.label: Low Risk
risk_bands.summary: Measured parameters are broadly consistent with people who did not develop diabetes in the reference cohort.
risk_bands.action: Maintain current diet and physical activity. Re-screen every 3 years, or annually from age 45.

risk_bands.label: Moderate Risk
risk_bands.summary: Several parameters sit in an intermediate range associated with impaired glucose regulation.
risk_bands.action: Request a fasting plasma glucose or HbA1c test at a registered clinic within the next 3 months. Begin structured lifestyle modification now.

risk_bands.label: High Risk
risk_bands.summary: The parameter profile closely matches people diagnosed with diabetes in the reference cohort.
risk_bands.action: Seek clinical assessment promptly. Ask specifically for a fasting plasma glucose, an oral glucose tolerance test, or an HbA1c measurement.

Pregnancies.measurement_note: Total number of times the patient has been pregnant.

bands.label: Typical
bands.note: Parity in this range carries no independent elevation of diabetes risk.

bands.label: High Parity
bands.note: High parity is associated with increased lifetime metabolic load and a greater chance of prior gestational diabetes.

Pregnancies.guideline: WHO recognises a history of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) as a major risk factor for later type 2 diabetes. Women with prior GDM should be screened at least every 3 years for life.
Pregnancies.source: WHO, Diagnostic Criteria and Classification of Hyperglycaemia First Detected in Pregnancy (2013)

Glucose.clinical_name: 2-hour plasma glucose during an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)
Glucose.measurement_note: Measured 2 hours after a 75 g oral glucose load. This is the single strongest predictor in the model.

bands.label: Normal Glucose Tolerance
bands.note: Below 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L).

bands.label: Impaired Glucose Tolerance
bands.note: 140-199 mg/dL (7.8-11.0 mmol/L). Classified by WHO as intermediate hyperglycaemia, commonly called prediabetes.

bands.label: Diabetes Range
bands.note: 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or above. Meets the WHO 2-hour OGTT threshold for diabetes and requires confirmatory testing.

Glucose.guideline: WHO defines diabetes at a 2-hour post-load plasma glucose of 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or above, and impaired glucose tolerance between 7.8 and 11.0 mmol/L (140-199 mg/dL). A single abnormal result must be confirmed on a separate day in a person without symptoms.
Glucose.source: WHO/IDF, Definition and Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus and Intermediate Hyperglycaemia (2006); WHO Classification of Diabetes Mellitus (2019)

BloodPressure.measurement_note: The lower number in a blood pressure reading. This dataset records diastolic pressure only, so a full hypertension classification is not possible from this field alone.

bands.label: Normal
bands.note: Below 80 mm Hg diastolic.

bands.label: High-Normal
bands.note: 80-89 mm Hg. Frequently accompanies insulin resistance as part of the metabolic syndrome.

bands.label: Hypertensive Range
bands.note: 90 mm Hg or above. Consistent with hypertension, which multiplies the cardiovascular risk carried by diabetes.

BloodPressure.guideline: WHO defines hypertension as a systolic pressure of 140 mm Hg or above and/or a diastolic pressure of 90 mm Hg or above, measured on two separate days. Hypertension and type 2 diabetes share insulin resistance as a common driver and frequently occur together.
BloodPressure.source: WHO Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Hypertension in Adults (2021)

SkinThickness.measurement_note: A caliper measurement of subcutaneous fat at the back of the upper arm, used as a proxy for body fat distribution.

bands.label: Within Typical Range
bands.note: Consistent with typical subcutaneous adiposity.

bands.label: Elevated Adiposity
bands.note: Suggests excess subcutaneous fat, which contributes to peripheral insulin resistance.

bands.label: High Adiposity
bands.note: Markedly elevated subcutaneous fat store.

SkinThickness.guideline: Skinfold thickness is not a WHO diagnostic criterion. It is used here as a supporting measure of adiposity alongside BMI, because body fat distribution modifies insulin sensitivity independently of total weight.
SkinThickness.source: Contextual reference; not a diagnostic threshold.

Insulin.measurement_note: Serum insulin measured 2 hours after a glucose load. High values alongside high glucose indicate insulin resistance rather than insulin deficiency.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: Below the usual post-load response. May indicate reduced pancreatic beta-cell output.

bands.label: Typical Post-Load Response
bands.note: Roughly 16-166 µU/mL is the commonly cited 2-hour reference interval.

bands.label: Hyperinsulinaemia
bands.note: A raised insulin level indicates the pancreas is compensating for peripheral insulin resistance, which often precedes type 2 diabetes by years.

Insulin.guideline: There is no WHO diagnostic cut-off for serum insulin, and the reference interval is laboratory-dependent. Persistent hyperinsulinaemia alongside normal glucose is an early marker of insulin resistance and precedes measurable hyperglycaemia.
Insulin.source: Laboratory reference interval; not a WHO diagnostic threshold.

BMI.measurement_note: Weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres. WHO standard cut-offs apply to African populations; the lower Asian-specific cut-offs are not used here.

bands.label: Underweight
bands.note: Below 18.5 kg/m2.

bands.label: Overweight
bands.note: 25.0-29.9 kg/m2. Risk of type 2 diabetes begins to rise steeply in this band.

bands.label: Obesity Class III
bands.note: 40.0 kg/m2 or above.

BMI.guideline: WHO classifies overweight as a BMI of 25 kg/m2 or above and obesity as 30 kg/m2 or above. Excess adiposity is the largest modifiable risk factor for type 2 diabetes. A sustained loss of 5-7% of body weight measurably reduces progression from prediabetes to diabetes.
BMI.source: WHO, Obesity and Overweight Fact Sheet; WHO Technical Report Series 894

DiabetesPedigreeFunction.measurement_note: A synthesised score summarising diabetes history among relatives, weighted by genetic relatedness and the age at which those relatives were diagnosed. It is specific to this dataset, not a laboratory test.

bands.label: Limited Family History
bands.note: Little recorded diabetes among close relatives.

bands.label: Moderate Family History
bands.note: Diabetes present among relatives, contributing measurable inherited risk.

bands.label: Strong Family History
bands.note: Substantial diabetes history among close relatives, or early-onset diagnoses.

DiabetesPedigreeFunction.guideline: A first-degree relative with type 2 diabetes roughly doubles a person's lifetime risk. IDF guidance places family history among the core non-modifiable risk factors used to trigger earlier screening.
DiabetesPedigreeFunction.source: Smith et al., ADAP learning algorithm (1988); IDF risk factor guidance

Age.measurement_note: Age in completed years. Beta-cell function declines gradually with age, independently of weight.

bands.label: Under 35
bands.note: Background population risk, unless other risk factors are present.

bands.label: 35 to 44
bands.note: Incidence begins to climb from the mid-thirties onward.

bands.label: 45 and above
bands.note: Routine screening is recommended from age 45 regardless of other risk factors.

Age.guideline: Diabetes incidence rises with age. Screening is recommended from age 45 for the general population, and earlier where overweight, hypertension, or a family history of diabetes are present.
Age.source: IDF Global Guideline for Type 2 Diabetes; WHO screening guidance

general_guidance.title: Confirm before concluding
general_guidance.body: No screening score is a diagnosis. WHO requires a laboratory-confirmed fasting plasma glucose, a 2-hour OGTT value, or an HbA1c measurement, repeated on a separate day in a person without symptoms, before diabetes can be diagnosed.

general_guidance.title: Lifestyle modification is first-line
general_guidance.body: WHO recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week, a diet limiting free sugars to under 10% of total energy intake, and a sustained 5-7% reduction in body weight for people carrying excess weight. Structured lifestyle programmes reduce progression from prediabetes to diabetes by roughly half.

general_guidance.title: Tobacco and alcohol
general_guidance.body: Tobacco use increases the risk of type 2 diabetes and accelerates its vascular complications. WHO advises cessation of tobacco use and moderation of alcohol intake as part of diabetes prevention.

general_guidance.title: Undiagnosed diabetes causes silent damage
general_guidance.body: Type 2 diabetes is frequently without symptoms for years while damage accumulates in the retina, kidneys, and peripheral nerves. Early detection is the primary reason screening exists.

notes: The IDF Diabetes Atlas estimates several million adults living with diabetes in Nigeria, and reports that Africa has the highest proportion of undiagnosed diabetes of any IDF region - the majority of cases are never identified.
Laboratory access is uneven outside major urban centres, so low-cost screening that runs on parameters obtainable at a primary health centre has practical value.
Rising urbanisation, reduced physical activity, and dietary transition are increasing type 2 diabetes incidence across West Africa.
WHO standard BMI cut-offs (overweight 25, obesity 30) apply to African populations. The lower Asian-specific cut-offs should not be substituted.
regional_context.source: IDF Diabetes Atlas; WHO Regional Office for Africa. Figures are indicative and should be checked against the current Atlas edition before citation.

disclaimer: This application is a statistical screening aid built for educational and early-detection purposes. It does not diagnose diabetes, does not replace a qualified clinician, and must not be used to start, stop, or alter any treatment. Anyone with symptoms or an elevated result should consult a licensed healthcare professional.
